articles.title: Wu Shicun on why Beijing will not rule out Scarborough Shoal construction
articles.summary:
- Wu Shicun, founding president of China's National Institute for South China Sea Studies, argues that the Philippines' "assertive transparency" strategy deliberately provokes confrontations (e.g., at Renai/Second Thomas Shoal and Sabina Shoal) and uses viral videos to frame China as the aggressor and the Philippines as the victim, partly to secure more budget and equipment from the Philippine Congress.

- China has primarily focused its diplomatic capital on rule-making rather than public narratives, advancing the Code of Conduct (COC) negotiations since 2013 and convening the 56th working group session on the Declaration on Conduct of Parties (DOC) implementation in Vietnam.

- Wu acknowledges China was initially caught off guard by the Philippines' media strategy, particularly during the 2023 Second Thomas Shoal stand-off and the Sabina Shoal intrusion, but has since adjusted by proactively countering Manila's narratives and exposing what it views as deliberate smearing campaigns backed by Western media.

- China is now shifting to a more proactive approach in constructing its own South China Sea narrative, a "profound paradigm shift" Wu says reflects lessons learned and is expected to intensify as China positions itself as a responsible major power.

articles.title: Zheng Yongnian on Trump, Venezuela and why China doesn’t want ‘a separate kitchen’
articles.summary:
• **Zheng Yongnian identifies Trump's "Donroe Doctrine" as a two-part strategy**: consolidating US influence in the western hemisphere by viewing Chinese and Russian presence as a national security threat, and executing genuine offshore balancing—a strategic contraction that was discussed but never fully implemented during the Obama era.

• **Zheng sees Venezuela as not an isolated target but part of a broader pattern**: right-wing US think tanks have discussed a tripartite partition of the world among major powers, paralleling Putin's long-standing approach to redrawing spheres of influence—raising fears among European nations that Ukraine may not be Russia's final objective either.

• **US withdrawal from existing global orders (Europe, Middle East, East Asia) will create local chaos, while its re-embedding in Latin America will cause similar disruption**—with turbulence as the defining trend regardless of whether the US retreats or advances, as significant structural adjustments will follow.

• **Zheng predicts rapid changes at three levels**: big-power relations (the primary driver of geopolitical shifts), the reassertion of "regional lords" like Turkey among Turkic-speaking states, and broader structural shifts in the world order—though he stops short of calling for a complete decoupling of the existing system.

articles.title: 80 years on from WWII, China’s interests lie in peaceful Asia-Pacific: Rana Mitter
articles.summary:
• Historian Rana Mitter argues WWII is one of the most important yet underestimated factors in shaping modern China, calling it the greatest political and economic trauma of the 20th century, with millions of deaths, mass internal displacement, and destruction of 1920s–1930s infrastructure.

• The devastation of the war made revolution more likely than reform, opening space for the Chinese Communist Party to expand in rural areas; systems like the work-unit model and greater public roles for women emerged during the war years.

• The war weakened rival warlords and advanced national unification, though solid unification was only achieved with the 1949 Communist revolution; WWII also remains significant as a symbol of unity among nationalists, communists, and others against a common external threat.

• Mitter suggests that as China prepares for the 80th anniversary of WWII's end, Beijing could leverage the occasion to improve people-to-people exchanges with the West, but criticizes China for often relying on complaint-focused diplomatic language rather than seizing broader opportunities.

articles.title: Liu Qian on Chinese innovation, the US rivalry and women holding up half the sky
articles.summary:
- **US-China rivalry extends beyond trade**: Liu Qian argues the rivalry now spans technology, ideologies, and global collaboration, warning that continued unhealthy competition will harm both countries and the world.

- **Trade protectionism concern is exaggerated**: Exports accounted for only about 19% of China's GDP last year, and US-bound exports represented roughly 2.8% of GDP — meaning even a total loss of the US export market would impact only 2–3% of China's economy.

- **China's export portfolio has diversified significantly**: ASEAN has overtaken the US as China's largest export destination. Exports to Brazil grew 23.3% last year, and exports to Africa rose 25.9% in the first eight months of this year, demonstrating successful market diversification.

- **Longer-term risks remain**: While exporters have shown resilience and adaptability, Liu Qian flags persistent concerns including unemployment hurting private consumption, business sentiment clouded by uncertainty, and supply chain adjustments.

- **Liu Qian's background**: She is the founder of Wusawa Advisory, former managing director of The Economist Group in Greater China, and the sole Chinese representative in the UN Women Leaders Network core working group, advocating for gender equality in policymaking.

articles.title: Fuchsia Dunlop tells how she fell for China’s cuisine and names her perfect dish
articles.summary:
- Fuchsia Dunlop is a British author and chef widely regarded as the Western world's foremost expert on Chinese regional cuisines, particularly Sichuanese food, having written seven books on the subject.

- Dunlop first traveled to China in 1994 as a British Council postgraduate student at Sichuan University, where she began studying cooking in local restaurant kitchens and at the Sichuan Higher Institute of Cuisine, eventually completing a three-month chef's training course with 50 local students.

- Upon returning to England, she identified a gap in the market—no English-language Sichuan cookbooks existed—and published her first book in 2001, noting how Sichuan food has since become widely popular in the West.

- She emphasizes the immense diversity and regional specificity of Chinese cuisine, from Cantonese lotus seed paste mooncakes to savory Shanghai minced pork varieties and Yunnan flaky-pastry versions with Yunnan ham, viewing writing about Chinese food as a way to explore the country's broader culture.

- Her enthusiasm has only deepened over the years, as she notes China's size and culinary diversity mean there is always more to discover, making it a lifelong area of research and writing.

articles.title: Kurt Campbell on US deterrence, the Quad, Aukus and Taiwan after Xi-Trump summit
articles.summary:
- **Kurt Campbell**, a veteran US diplomat known as the Biden administration's "Asia tsar," served in key Indo-Pacific policy roles from 2009 to 2025 and was a key architect of the "pivot to Asia," the Quad, and the "small yard, high fence" technology strategy against China.

- Campbell states that both US and Chinese leaders have a mutual interest in **stabilizing the bilateral relationship**, driven by both a desire to improve competitive advantage and a willingness to work together on select issues.

- He warns that **Trump is neglecting alliances** in favor of prioritizing the China relationship, citing the deteriorating US-Canada relationship — including Canada's reported interest in joining the EU — as particularly troubling and counterproductive to American global influence.

- Campbell maintains his longstanding argument that **US strength depends on allied scale** rather than unilateral dominance, arguing that sustaining the global order and technology strategy requires a strong posture with both China *and* allies and partners simultaneously.

articles.title: South Korea wants free ‘AI for All’. Is society ready?
articles.summary:
• South Korea is launching an ambitious "AI for All" initiative under President Lee Jae Myung, planning to provide every citizen with free, unlimited access to general-purpose AI chatbots and agents, integrating AI into hospitals, schools, government offices, and daily life. A beta version is set to launch this month, with AI developers led by SK Telecom, KT, and Kakao using hundreds of Nvidia B200 GPUs provided by the government.

• The government has a 10 trillion won (US$7.3 billion) AI budget for the current fiscal year, with an additional 250 billion won allocated for the rollout through 2027. From next year, the trial is intended to become a permanent, taxpayer-funded public utility connected to government systems for services like booking medical appointments, house hunting, and tax advice via AI intermediaries.

• To manage risks, South Korea is relying on its AI Basic Act (effective January) requiring human-in-the-loop oversight, mandatory impact assessments, and synthetic content watermarking. A state-funded AI Safety Institute has been established as a technical watchdog, and the government plans an autonomous reliability-assurance system based on seven AI Ethics Principles including accountability, privacy protection, and fairness.

• The initiative represents a stark contrast to warnings from leading AI figures—including Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and Geoffrey Hinton—about existential risks of unchecked AI development. While Silicon Valley debates slowing down, Seoul is deliberately "hitting the accelerator," aiming to lower access barriers so AI benefits are distributed evenly rather than concentrated among a few.

articles.title: Hong Kong’s historic vessels sail into the future
articles.summary:
• The Hong Kong Historic Vessels Foundation (HKHVF), officially founded in 2024, owns and maintains five historic vessels, including Way Foong (built 1930 by the Hong Kong and Whampoa Dock Company for HSBC) and Java (built 1935, formerly a government vessel known as Marine 1), to preserve the city's maritime heritage.

• Way Foong served as a ferry, tugboat, and employee pleasure craft for HSBC for over 70 years before entering private ownership; Java was used to transport VIPs, conduct anti-piracy patrols, and tow buoys, earning a reputation as "almost unsinkable" due to its Burmese-teak construction with deck planks nearly 4.5cm thick.

• Java became the foundation's first acquisition after a future co-founder spotted it in Tai Tam Harbour in the early 2000s; this purchase inspired subsequent acquisitions and the eventual founding of the HKHVF.

• The organisation's historians have identified nine pre-1950s boats built in Hong Kong in various states of repair — some in the HKHVF collection, others privately owned, and one (Mon Lei) whose whereabouts remain unknown.

articles.title: Southeast Asia battles Big Tech to protect children online
articles.summary:
- Indonesia has implemented some of Southeast Asia's strictest rules banning under-16s from "high-risk" social media, prompting Meta, YouTube, and TikTok to raise minimum ages to 16 and deactivate underage accounts; TikTok alone deactivated 9 million underage accounts in Indonesia by October, and Roblox introduced facial age-scanning for users.

- Despite these measures, age restrictions remain largely ineffective because young users can easily bypass them by lying about their age at registration; Indonesia's government has given tech companies until the end of the year to complete comprehensive self-assessments of their age-verification, algorithm, and ad-targeting systems.

- If platforms fail to comply, Indonesia has finalized a sanctions mechanism that would allow fines of up to 6% of tech firms' global revenue — roughly US$12 billion based on Meta's reported 2025 revenue.

- This follows a precedent set in August, when Meta agreed to pay up to US$18 billion to settle US state lawsuits alleging its platforms were deliberately designed to make children addicted, with sweeping changes including daily usage limits, overnight usage blocks, and strengthened age-verification controls.

- Governments across Southeast Asia — from Malaysia to Vietnam, the Philippines, and Singapore — are shifting from urging Big Tech to protect children to imposing enforceable rules, signaling a broader regional regulatory trend; Meta has migrated approximately 22.5 million Indonesian users to "teen accounts," though Indonesia's government considers this insufficient.

articles.title: Talk is growing of a Tesla-SpaceX merger. Will geopolitics throw a spanner in the works?
articles.summary:
• **Tesla's Gigafactory in Shanghai produces vehicles at a 40-second assembly cycle and exported more than half of its output overseas as of July 2025**, with a record 7,738 vehicles shipped on a single vessel, making China a critical hub for Tesla's global supply chain.

• **Elon Musk faces a geopolitical balancing act**, as his EV business relies heavily on China's supply chain while SpaceX has become a core US national security contractor for the Pentagon, creating tension between Washington and Beijing interests.

• **Growing speculation surrounds a potential Tesla-SpaceX merger** driven by deepening technology overlap in AI, robotics, and logistics; Musk has neither confirmed nor denied the rumors, while Wall Street analysts note the two firms are increasingly becoming suppliers to each other.

• **A merger would heighten national-security sensitivities**, as SpaceX's close ties to the US government would intersect with Tesla's extensive China operations, requiring a complex ring-fenced strategy to satisfy regulators in both countries.

• **Industry observers warn the current geopolitical landscape poses significant risk to Musk's multi-track approach**, with the danger of maintaining balance intensifying if the businesses are brought closer together.

articles.title: Antwerp: a well-seasoned melting pot of Rubens, diamonds and Belgium’s only Chinatown
articles.summary:
• Antwerp (population 568,000) is a major cultural destination, home to Baroque painter Peter Paul Rubens, Renaissance-era architecture, and the Royal Museum of Fine Arts, which houses works by masters ranging from Jan van Eyck to René Magritte.

• The city is a diverse multicultural hub: Jewish immigrants from the late 15th century established it as a global diamond trade centre; post-WWII settlers from China created Belgium's only official Chinatown; and recent refugees from Afghanistan, Syria, Iraq, Somalia, and Ukraine continue to add to its cosmopolitan character.

• Around 120 diamond and gold jewellery boutiques are concentrated within a single square mile near the city's Central Station—a late-19th-century building often awarded "World's Most Beautiful Station"—creating a striking juxtaposition of Chinatown's pagoda gate and an Orthodox Jewish community on adjacent streets.

• Antwerp is located just 40 minutes by train from Brussels and is easily accessible, yet retains distinct neighbourhoods where different languages (such as Yiddish) and traditions coexist in close proximity.

articles.title: Thailand has had enough of foreign tourists behaving badly
articles.summary:
- **Tourism recovery remains below pre-pandemic levels**: Thailand attracted nearly 40 million visitors in 2019, but last year's total fell to 32.9 million, and the Tourism Authority of Thailand has further trimmed its 2026 forecast to 30–34 million, citing rising oil prices, higher airfares from geopolitical conflicts, and a strong baht driving budget travelers to Vietnam and Malaysia.

- **Structural shift from group tours to independent travel**: The post-pandemic decline in large Chinese and other organized tour groups has hit businesses like the Samut Prakan Crocodile Farm & Zoo hard, which saw its daily influx of 100–200 tour buses drop to a handful; the broader trend is toward "free, independent tourists" (FITs), reshaping tourism infrastructure and revenue models across Thailand.

- **Tourism is economically critical**: The industry accounts for roughly one-fifth of Thailand's economy, spanning everything from five-star resorts in Phuket and Koh Samui to street-level operators in Pattaya.

- **Rising tourist misbehavior is eroding Thai patience**: Years of foreign tourists engaging in disrespectful or unlawful behavior have worn thin on locals, contributing to a political and social pushback that adds another headwind to Thailand's tourism recovery efforts.

articles.title: Going ‘car-lite’: why more Singaporeans are quitting driving
articles.summary:
- **COE prices have skyrocketed**, making car ownership increasingly unaffordable: the Certificate of Entitlement (COE) cost around S$10,000 in 2006, rose to S$50,000 by 2016, and now exceeds S$112,000 (US$87,400) for a 10-year renewal, prompting many Singaporeans to give up their cars.

- **Private car numbers are declining**: Land Transport Authority data from July showed 516,237 privately owned cars on the road — the lowest since 2019 — though private cars still make up 79% of all vehicles, with rental, ride-hailing, and corporate car shares increasing.

- **Rising running costs compound the problem**, including higher road tax, fuel, maintenance, and insurance, alongside Singapore's Electronic Road Pricing (ERP) congestion-charging system, which has recently been reinstated in areas like Orchard Road for the first time since 2020.

- **Singapore's "Move Lite" campaign**, launched in 2022 by the Land Transport Authority, promotes walking, cycling, and public transport as sustainable alternatives to driving; its messaging has shifted from highlighting public transport benefits to spotlighting the downsides of driving, such as congestion and parking difficulties.

- **The government's broader strategy** aims to create a "car-lite" society by investing in public transport and active mobility infrastructure while managing vehicle ownership and road usage to make efficient use of limited land — though officials say the goal is to expand mobility options rather than prioritize or discourage any specific group of commuters.

articles.title: Chinese brokers work to crack the final code: win clients on global stage
articles.summary:
- Chinese investment banks shifted from emulating Wall Street firms like Goldman Sachs to pursuing a broader ambition under President Xi Jinping's 2023 call to build first-class institutions and become a "financial superpower with distinct Chinese characteristics."

- China now operates the world's second-largest capital market, and in 2025 direct financing through stocks and bonds surpassed bank lending for the first time, creating strong domestic growth conditions for Chinese securities firms.

- Chinese brokerages are increasingly expanding internationally, with Hong Kong serving as a key growth hub, driven by its expanding role in China's capital markets and mainland companies' aggressive overseas investments.

- The industry's evolution traces back to the 1995 establishment of CICC, the first Sino-foreign joint-venture investment bank, which initially relied heavily on Western partners for expertise and access—evidenced by Goldman Sachs training CICC executives ahead of the landmark US$4.2 billion China Mobile listing in 1997.

articles.title: From kitchen waste to sky-high costs: inside Hong Kong’s quest for green jet fuel
articles.summary:
• **"Gutter oil" (recycled kitchen/drainage waste) has become a valuable feedstock for producing sustainable aviation fuel (SAF)**, shifting from a free commodity to one whose unit cost now exceeds conventional fuel, according to Hong Kong-based producer EcoCeres.

• **SAF can reduce life-cycle carbon emissions by up to 80%** compared with conventional jet fuel and is a "drop-in" substitute requiring no engine modifications, but its high price remains the primary barrier to adoption.

• **Hong Kong's Chief Executive John Lee revised the city's 2030 SAF target to 1–3%** (from an initial 1–2%) of all fuel used by departing flights and pledged to develop a competitive SAF value chain in the Greater Bay Area; however, the government has yet to clarify who will bear the cost.

• **Industry players describe the 1–3% target as "fairly cautious"** and achievable, as Asian economies typically set 2030 SAF targets of 1–5%; some expect Hong Kong to serve as a pilot site for mainland China to test market responses before broader rollout.

• **Airlines and producers are calling for clearer policy direction**, with Cathay Pacific's CEO noting that producer confidence, affordable fuel supply for airlines, and investor policy clarity must all be addressed through well-designed regulation.

commentary:
# 旅游业出口依赖与泰国资本主义的结构性困境

## 一、现象描述

泰国旅游业因游客行为失范、地缘冲突推高成本及泰铢走强，国际游客数量持续下滑，经济遭受外部冲击。

## 二、政治经济学定位

泰国旅游业占其经济总量约五分之一，这一数据远非一个普通的产业结构指标，而是深刻揭示了泰国在全球资本主义体系中的依附性定位。旅游业本质上是一种服务业的出口贸易——泰国出售的是本国劳动者的劳动力使用价值、自然资源和国土空间的使用权，以换取国际货币资本的流入。马克思在《资本论》第一卷中指出："资本主义生产不仅是商品的生产，它实质上是剩余价值的生产。"泰国旅游业的"商品"看似是服务体验，实则是泰国劳动者在旅游资本支配下所生产出的剩余价值的国际转移。酒店服务员的劳动、鳄鱼农场的驯兽表演、按摩师的技艺——这些劳动力的使用在旅游资本的增殖过程中被系统性地压低至劳动力价值的补偿线附近。当文章描述查隆所经营的鳄鱼农场——一家创立于九十多年前、从鳄鱼皮销售转型为旅游表演的企业——的门票收入日趋萎缩时，我们看到的不仅是一家企业的衰落，更是依附于国际消费需求波动的整个社会生产体系的脆弱性。

## 三、深层结构分析

泰国经济对旅游业的深度依赖，是全球资本主义国际分工体系下半外围国家畸形产业结构的典型表征。正如马克思所论述的工场手工业"通过手工业活动的分解、劳动工具的专门化，造成了社会生产过程的质的划分和量的比例"，泰国的经济结构也经历了类似的"专门化"过程——大量社会资本和劳动力被"专门化"地配置到旅游服务部门，而国内制造业和农业的自主发展则相应地被挤压。"工场手工业同时也损害了工人的整个劳动能力，使工人畸形发展"，这一论断同样适用于国家层面：泰国经济的"旅游化"使整个社会的生产能力呈现出畸形发展——大量劳动力从事的不是具有更高生产率的物质生产部门，而是以接待和取悦外国消费者为核心的低附加值服务业。文章所揭示的外部冲击周期——SARS、禽流感、金融危机、新冠疫情、俄乌冲突——恰恰证明了这种依附性经济结构的根本脆弱性。当"价值形成过程"因外部需求骤降而被迫中断时，整个社会再生产体系便面临崩溃的危险。

## 四、阶级与利益分析

在这一体系中，谁受益、谁受损？国际航空运营商和全球旅游资本是第一层受益者——它们通过控制交通和分销渠道，截取了国际游客消费的相当份额。泰国本土旅游业资本家——大型度假村所有者、连锁酒店集团——构成第二层受益者。而真正承受劳动剥削的，是无数酒店服务员、小商贩、按摩从业者和像查隆这样的小企业主——他们既受国际资本的挤压，又承受着本国资本的层层盘剥。当游客行为"失范"时，冲突首先爆发在旅游劳动者与外国消费者之间，而这一表象掩盖了双方共同受制于旅游资本积累逻辑的结构性事实。

## 五、主流叙事批判

文章及主流舆论将问题的核心框定为"游客素质下降"，这实质上是一种将结构性矛盾转化为文化道德问题的叙事策略。泰国社会对"失范游客"的愤怒固然有其文化合理性的维度，但从政治经济学角度看，这一叙事遮蔽了真正的矛盾——一个国家的经济命脉被系于外国消费者反复无常的需求之上，其劳动者被迫将自身尊严和身体作为商品出售给来自富裕国家的购买者——这本身就是不平等交换关系的极端表现。"泰国人很务实。我们确实喜欢旅游业带来的钱，"评论人士的这一表述恰恰揭示了这一交易关系的残酷本质：以国家尊严和人民尊严换取国际货币，这不是什么自由选择，而是全球资本主义体系下依附性发展的必然结果。

## 六、解放前景

从政治经济学角度审视，泰国旅游业的困境并非靠提高"服务质量"或加强"游客管理"所能根本解决的。出路在于打破对旅游出口的依附性结构：国家应将积累的旅游外汇资本投向具有自主发展能力的物质生产部门；旅游劳动者应通过集体组织提高其在劳动过程中的议价能力；更重要的是，必须认识到在资本主义世界体系中，任何将一国经济命脉寄托于外部消费的模式都终将面临周期性危机。正如马克思所揭示的，资本主义生产的核心矛盾在于其社会化生产与私人占有之间的内在张力——泰国旅游业的困境，不过是这一矛盾在全球尺度上的又一次展开。唯有在根本上改变泰国在全球分工体系中的从属地位，实现生产力的自主发展与劳动者的全面解放，才能终结这一依附性循环。
